中提琴主要由木材構成，琴身採用雲杉木製作面板，背板與側板則使用楓木，具有良好的音: The viola is made mainly of wood: the top is spruce, the back and ribs maple, all with good acoustic properties. The neck is of hard maple, and the fingerboard is usually ebony, for durability and appearance. The strings are mostly gut or synthetic, with the upper strings wound with aluminium, silver or other metal wire. The bow is made of wood, horsehair and metal fittings, and together they produce the viola's characteristic warm tone.
中提琴以弓拉弦發聲，持琴方式與小提琴相同，置於左肩與臉側之間，但因琴身較大，手臂: The viola is sounded by drawing the bow across the strings, and it is held as the violin is, between the left shoulder and the side of the face; because the body is larger, players with shorter arms should choose a smaller size. The four strings, from low to high, are C3, G3, D4 and A4. Tune the A string first to 440 to 442 Hz, then tune the others in fifths, with a tuner or a piano to help. Beginners must note that the strings are thicker and respond more slowly, so the bow has to start earlier and bear more weight; the left hand mostly stops the strings with the pads of the fingers, the finger spacing is wider, half position and third position are common, and the left elbow has to reach forward or round towards the lowest string for a clear tone.
中提琴屬弦鳴樂器，以弓擦弦發聲，空弦由低到高為C3、G3、D4、A4，音域比小提: The viola is a chordophone sounded by drawing a bow across the strings; its open strings from low to high are C3, G3, D4 and A4, and its range is a perfect fifth below the violin and an octave above the cello. Its strings are thicker than the violin's and its soundbox larger, so the tone is lower than the violin's and more veiled than the cello's. Response is slower, and the player needs heavier bow pressure and an earlier bow stroke to control volume and attack; the wider hair and heavier bow also demand more arm weight and a wider finger spacing. Compared with the rest of the family it shares the G, D and A strings with the violin, yet its tone is softer and deeper, and it usually takes an inner part.
中提琴屬弦鳴樂器，名稱源自義大利語，早期在歐洲與義大利發展，尺寸與名稱亦隨音域需: The viola is a chordophone whose name comes from Italian; it developed early in Europe and Italy, and its size and name changed with the demands of range. Before the mid-eighteenth century it was used mainly in the orchestra, often taking the harmony and occasionally doubling the melody; Bach's Brandenburg Concerto No. 6 gives the main melody to two violas. After the mid-eighteenth century, with the rise of the string quartet, it became a central voice in chamber music, and solo playing gradually spread, for example Berlioz's Harold in Italy and Stamitz's Concerto in D major. In the twentieth century, through players such as Tertis, composers wrote more for the viola, and it also appears in avant-garde music, jazz and Hungarian and Romanian folk bands.

Before the mid-eighteenth century it was used only in the orchestra; afterwards, with the rise of the string quartet, it became a central voice in chamber music, and only in the second half of the eighteenth century did it become at all common as a solo instrument. You can listen to Stamitz's Viola Concerto in D major, Berlioz's Harold in Italy, Bach's Brandenburg Concerto No. 6, Mozart's string quintets, and the sixth variation, Ysobel, in Elgar's Enigma Variations. In folk music, Hungarian and Romanian Transylvanian bands include a three-string viola; contemporary popular music, avant-garde and jazz also use it occasionally.

The viola is a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 321.322-71, a member of the violin family, usually played with a bow. Its construction is close to the violin's but the body is larger, and there is no single standard size; a full-size body is about one to four inches longer than a violin's, about sixteen inches on average. Its four strings are tuned from low to high to C3, G3, D4 and A4, a perfect fifth below the violin. The player, called a violist, holds the instrument between the left shoulder and the chin; because the strings are thicker and the bow heavier, it takes more force to stop the strings and to draw the bow. It is commonly used in the orchestra, the string quartet and chamber music, and also appears in folk music, popular music and jazz.
